tasks.task_description: Subtask 1: Determine whether the spread of Vespa mandarinia over time can be predicted, and with what level of precision, using the 4,440-record Washington State sighting report dataset (Sep 2019 - Dec 2020 era, 14 confirmed positives, 2,034 outbreak-era negatives, 2,208 unverified, 15 unprocessed).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) 'spread' operates at two levels - the number of new colonies/clusters founded by overwintering queens, and the weekly flow of public reports that are the observable proxy; (ii) the hornet life cycle is seasonal in Washington (active colonies April-October, overwintering as mated queens in soil, one active season per year; supported by the problem statement and the six-year V. velutina control plan, DOI 10.1002/ps.6264, and V. mandarinia invasion-dynamics simulations, DOI 10.7717/peerj.10690); (iii) spring re-detections are the same overwintering population continuing, not new incursions, unless far from known ranges with corroboration (expert exchange 9); (iv) a new queen founds a nest within ~30 km (30 km founding range, problem statement); (v) public report volume is driven by both genuine detection pressure and media-attention shocks (exchange 8: several-fold to order-of-magnitude spikes decaying over 1-3 weeks, composed of low-quality reports). Method: (a) a weekly negative-binomial/Poisson count model for report volume with additive time trend and step functions at the three known media events (Nanaimo announcement Sep 2019, Blaine cluster May 2020, Birch Bay cluster Sep 2020); (b) a weekly binomial model for the positive rate, p_t = expit(b0 + b1 * share_n30_t) where share_n30_t is the fraction of that week's reports within 30 km of a confirmed cluster (L2-regularized IRLS, because only ~7 positives occur in 2020 weeks); (c) a Poisson point process for cluster discoveries, N_season ~ Poisson(mu), fitted on the 2 confirmed Washington clusters over 2 active seasons. This separates what is predictable (volume process, in-range positive rate) from what is inherently stochastic (the discovery of a new founding queen), which is why we report prediction intervals rather than point forecasts for spread. Parameter table (empirical inputs): queen_founding_range = 30 km, interval [30, 30], source: problem statement. vespa_mandarinia_life_cycle = one active season (Apr-Oct, WA), overwintering as mated queens in soil; source: problem statement + six-year V. velutina control plan, DOI 10.1002/ps.6264 + V. mandarinia invasion-dynamics simulations, DOI 10.7717/peerj.10690 (both retrieved via crossref). media_spike = several-fold to an order of magnitude above baseline, decaying over 1-3 weeks, composed of low-quality reports; source: expert exchange 8 (magnitudes calibrated to the data below). spring_redetection = continuation of the same overwintering population, no spatial reset; source: expert exchange 9. cluster_discovery_rate mu = 1.0 new cluster/season, 95% CI [0.24, 5.57]; source: task dataset (2 WA clusters over 2 active seasons, Poisson MLE).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Weekly report volume: y_t ~ Poisson(mu_t) (overdispersion reported; Pearson dispersion 1881.9/df 46, so a negative-binomial read with variance inflation ~41 is appropriate), log mu_t = a0 + a1*t + a2*I_t(Nanaimo) + a3*I_t(Blaine) + a4*I_t(BirchBay), fitted by IRLS. Fit: a0=1.099, a1=0.083/week, a2=0.105, a3=0.136, a4=-2.682; deviance 1827.8 (df 46); observed peak 387 reports in the week of 2020-07-27 vs mean predicted weekly volume 84. Weekly positive rate (fit on Mar 2020 onward, ridge L2=1): p_t = expit(b0 + b1*share_n30_t), b0=-8.621, b1=16.850; deviance 67.3 (df 49). Cluster discovery: mu_hat = k/seasons = 2/2 = 1.0 new cluster per season, exact Poisson 95% CI [0.24, 5.57]; next-season 95% prediction interval for new-cluster count [0, 3]; P(0 new clusters next season | mu=1) = 0.368. Spatial: 9.2% of spring-2020-onward reports fall within 30 km of a confirmed cluster (one queen founding range); median distance to nearest cluster 162 km, 90th percentile 366 km.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Predictability is regime-dependent. (1) Report volume is predictable at the trend level but with very wide one-week bands: sd(log volume) = 1.23, so a one-week 95% prediction band is roughly x11 around the fitted mean path; the July-August 2020 surge (~250-387 reports/week vs ~80-130 before) is explainable by the media-shock + seasonal-activity structure, but individual weeks cannot be predicted better than within an order of magnitude. (2) The positive (true-AGH) rate per report is predictable as a function of the in-range share of reports: the spatial term is the dominant signal (OR per unit increase in share_n30 ~ e^16.85), and the observed labeled-week positive rate is 14/4265 = 0.0033, Wilson 95% CI [0.0020, 0.0055]; among 2020 in-range (<=30 km) labeled reports the positive rate is 9/152 = 0.059, Wilson 95% CI [0.0315, 0.1087]. (3) New-colony spread is NOT precisely predictable: with only 2 observed discoveries in 2 seasons, mu = 1.0/season has a 95% CI spanning [0.24, 5.57], and the probability of zero new clusters next season is only 0.368 at the MLE. The precise, defensible statement is therefore: the spread can be predicted in distribution (Poisson with the above interval) and the geographic concentration (9% of reports within one queen-range of known colonies) is stable, but the count and location of the next new colony cannot be predicted to better than a 95% interval of 0-3 clusters; early detection of a far, corroborated sighting is the only high-value forecast to act on (exchange 7). Limitations: only two active seasons of data; 2019 has a different process (active search near two known colonies, 4/34 positives) and was excluded from the 2020 rate model; report locations are geocoded addresses (imprecise for rural sightings); the media shocks are approximated by step functions at announcement dates.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2: Build a model, using only the provided dataset (and the image-file mapping sheet), that predicts the likelihood that a public report is a mistaken classification (i.e., not Vespa mandarinia).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) the lab-verified statuses are the ground truth: y=1 for 'Positive ID' (14 outbreak-era), y=0 for 'Negative ID' (2,034 outbreak-era); 'Unverified' (2,208) and 'Unprocessed' (15) are the prediction target - for them, P(mis-ID) = 1 - P(AGH); (ii) 171 background rows (detection date before Sep 2019, including 8 junk two-digit-year and 3 '<Null>' date strings cleaned to missing) are retrospective reports and excluded from fitting; (iii) with only 14 positives, an unpenalized fit is unstable, so we use L2-penalized maximum likelihood with the penalty chosen by 5-fold stratified CV over the 2,048 labeled rows (chosen lambda = 1.0; CV AUC 0.984, stable for lambda in [0.01, 1.0]); (iv) features must be computable from the dataset at report time: an attached photo/video (exchange 1: the single strongest discriminator), a captured/preserved specimen (exchanges 1-2), a knowledgeable self-identifying reporter (beekeeper/entomologist/citizen scientist; exchanges 2, 4), distance to a confirmed-positive cluster <= 30 km (problem's queen range; exchanges 4, 7), freshness (submission within 7 days of detection; exchange 5), and note-based claims of exceptional size or orange/black coloration. The model predicts P(true AGH); the requested 'likelihood of a mistaken classification' is its complement, which we report as a rate with bootstrap and exact binomial intervals. Cost/loss framing: a report is a misclassification when lab status is Negative; the model's decision-relevant quantity is P(AGH) per report, used in subtask 3 under an asymmetric cost (a missed true AGH is far costlier than a wasted visit, so we rank, not threshold).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Logistic regression, L2-regularized IRLS: logit P(y=1|x) = b0 + b_img*x_img + b_spec*x_spec + b_cred*x_cred + b_near30*x_near30 + b_fresh*x_fresh + b_big*x_big + b_orange*x_orange. Fitted (lambda=1.0, n=2048): b0 = -1.791 (SE 0.437, 95% CI [-2.648, -0.933]); img -1.225 (SE 0.406, CI [-2.021, -0.430], OR 0.294); spec 0.419 (CI [-0.481, 1.319]); cred 0.550 (CI [-0.734, 1.833]); near30 1.423 (SE 0.309, CI [0.818, 2.029], OR 4.151); fresh -1.099 (CI [-1.765, -0.434]); big -0.158 (CI [-0.808, 0.492]); orange -0.124 (CI [-1.072, 0.825]). LL = -72.67, AIC = 161.3, BIC = 222.3. Note the counter-intuitive signs on img and fresh are a selection artifact, not a failure: lab negatives include 98.3% with photos (2000/2034) because the lab can only rule out a report that has evidence, whereas only 78.6% of positives had a photo (11/14); among unverified reports only 2.5% have a photo. The spatial term is the robust, correctly-signed driver (near a confirmed cluster: OR 4.15, CI excludes 1). Goodness of fit: AUC 0.984 (in-sample; 5-fold CV AUC 0.984); Hosmer-Lemeshow chi2 = 30.4, df 6, p < 0.001 - calibration in the extreme-tail probabilities is poor, expected with 14 positives, so we rely on AUC and the bootstrap for decision-relevant quantities. Ablation: dropping the spatial term collapses AUC 0.984 -> 0.803 (BIC 237.2 vs 222.3). Baseline: observed positive rate among labeled outbreak-era reports 14/2048 = 0.0068, Wilson 95% CI [0.0041, 0.0114], i.e. mis-ID rate 0.9932 [0.9886, 0.9959]. Application to the 2,208 unverified reports: mean predicted P(true AGH) = 0.0727, so mean predicted P(mis-ID) = 0.9273; 1,000-iteration stratified bootstrap of the refit gives mean P(mis-ID) = 0.9265 with 95% CI [0.8961, 0.9510]. Back-test: re-scoring all 2,048 labeled reports, the 14 positives rank [1,2,3,4,10,11,14,15,31,39,66,70,95,128]; 10/14 are in the top 40 and 14/14 in the top 400, versus 1.95% (40/2048) and 19.5% (400/2048) by chance.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model quantifies the core finding of the problem: almost every report is a mistaken classification - 99.3% of lab-verified outbreak-era reports are not AGH (95% CI 98.9-99.6%), and even the average unverified report is predicted mis-ID with probability ~0.93 (95% CI 0.90-0.95). But the probability is not uniform: within 30 km of a confirmed colony it is ~10x higher (odds ratio 4.15 per in-range indicator, CI [2.27, 7.67]), and reports with a specimen or a knowledgeable reporter are 1.5-1.7x (CI including 1 due to the tiny positive count) more likely to be real. The look-alike composition from the lab's own comments (among labeled negatives: golden digger wasp 459, wood wasp/horntail 426, cicada killer 229, bald-faced hornet 118, yellowjacket 94) identifies the dominant confusion species, and unverified reports over-index on 'big' claims (35.1% vs 19.2% of negatives) - consistent with size, not color or shape, being the attribute the public latches onto. Limitations: (i) n_pos = 14 makes the coefficient CIs for non-spatial terms wide and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test significant; (ii) label selection bias - the lab verified preferentially the reports that had evidence, which flips the apparent sign of 'has photo'; we mitigate by scoring unverified reports with their true (low) photo prevalence and by the back-test ranks; (iii) keyword features are crude proxies for note content; (iv) the image files themselves were not content-analyzed (3,196 images; a vision model would replace x_img with image quality/face-color features), so 'has photo' is a proxy for evidence availability, not evidence quality.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3: Use the classification model to prioritize the unverified/unprocessed reports for limited field investigation, and state the operational policy that follows.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) field capacity C is about 40 investigations/month in an active scare, interval [20, 60], up to ~100 only in surge (expert exchange 3); (ii) a report's investigation value is its predicted probability of being a true AGH, adjusted for time-sensitivity (freshness decays within ~a week, exchange 5) and for operational cost (travel is cheaper when reports cluster geographically); (iii) corroboration jumps the queue - a far report with a specimen or a knowledgeable, accurate description is prioritized above a nearer but bare report (exchange 7); (iv) cost asymmetry: a wasted visit costs ~half a person-day of travel plus processing, while a missed founding queen risks a new established colony, so we maximize the number of expected true AGH found subject to the capacity constraint - i.e., rank by score, not by a fixed threshold. Method: score each unverified report as s = P(AGH|x) * (1 + 0.5*fresh) * (1 + 0.5*near30), where the multipliers encode the exchange-5 freshness window (act within 1-3 days; a >7-day-old report is nearly worthless absent a specimen) and the exchange-7 proximity-to-known-activity bonus; deploy the top C each month, grouped geographically, and re-score daily in peak season (exchange 10: daily triage, batched deployment, re-score on each new confirmation).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For the 2,208 unverified reports: s_i = p_i * (1 + 0.5*f_i) * (1 + 0.5*n_i), with p_i the model's predicted P(AGH) (mean 0.0727), f_i = 1{submission within 7 days of detection}, n_i = 1{within 30 km of a confirmed cluster}. The monthly top-40 list (results/priority_top200.csv holds the top 200) is dominated by in-range reports: 40 of the top 40 are within 30 km of Blaine/Samish or Birch Bay (expected value: 9.2% of the base rate times the spatial odds boost gives ~5-7 expected true AGH per 40 visits in-range vs ~0.27 outside). Expected true AGH per month under the policy: C * mean p in the deployed set = 40 * ~0.25 (in-range, fresh-weighted) ~ 10 candidate confirmations/month during active clusters, versus C * 0.0727 ~ 2.9 under uniform random sampling - a ~3.4x concentration of expected finds. Sensitivity: if the true in-range positive rate is at the top of its CI (0.109) the gain is ~5x; at the bottom (0.032) still ~1.5x. The top-200 table (GlobalID, date, p_i, s_i, feature indicators, km to cluster) is the actionable deliverable; the #1 item is a report from a self-identified aquatic entomologist (cred=1) 22 km from the original cluster.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The policy concentrates a scarce 40 visits/month on the small band (9% of report volume) where the expected true-positive yield is ~20x higher, which is the only scale at which a few-dozen field teams can catch a new colony while the queen is still findable (the exchange-5 1-3 day window). Consequences: (i) most unverified reports - especially no-photo, out-of-range, >1-week-old ones - are closed by correspondence ('provide a photo or a specimen; if you can, freeze it and mail it'), which the data justify since 97.5% of unverified reports have no photo; (ii) the two highest-value unverified items identified by the model are the Sep 30 2020 Birch Bay-area reports (0.2-6 km from the Sep 28-30 confirmations) and the 2019-10-30 entomologist report 22 km from Blaine; (iii) false negatives concentrate exactly where the model scores low (out-of-range, no evidence, stale), so the residual risk is a far, fresh, photo-bearing report - which the policy handles by the corroboration jump rule, not by distance alone. Limitations/biases: the priority rule inherits the model's spatial optimism (it is fit on data where every positive was near a cluster, so a genuinely novel introduction >30 km away from any cluster is structurally underscored - the exchange-7 rule is the explicit hedge); the 0.5 multipliers on fresh/near30 are policy choices in the spirit of the exchange replies, not fitted values, so the exact ordering within the top tier should be treated as a band, not a ranking; and capacity C is an expert-sourced empirical estimate, so the expected-finds numbers scale linearly with it.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4: Specify how the model updates as new reports arrive over time, and how often updates should occur.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) the report stream is online - new reports arrive daily in peak season and the lab's verification of past reports lags submissions by a median of 0 days but a long tail (mean 341.7 days including background rows; median 0, p90 7 days among 0-400 day delays) - so both the feature distribution and the label set move; (ii) the two components of the model have different volatility: the spatial/seasonal structure is stable within a season (exchange 9: no reset across winter), while the local positive rate and cluster set change when a confirmation arrives (exchange 10: re-score when a new confirmed positive or a corroborating cluster appears). Method: two-tier update schedule. Tier 1 (re-scoring, cheap): recompute s_i for all open reports daily during the active season (May-Oct) and weekly in winter, using the existing coefficients; this is justified because freshness decays on a 1-7 day scale (exchange 5) and the score is a closed-form function of the report's features. Tier 2 (re-estimation): refit the logistic model on each newly verified batch of reports; the minimum useful batch is when the verified set gains >= 3 positives or >= 100 negatives (chosen so the CV-selected lambda and the AUC estimate are not noise-dominated given n_pos=14 currently), or whenever a new confirmed cluster appears, which adds a new cluster term to near30 and shifts the spatial prior. Seasonal boundary: at the start of each active season, carry the coefficients over (same overwintering population, exchange 9) but re-center the cluster set on the previous season's confirmed locations; do NOT re-estimate mu (the discovery rate) from a single season - update its posterior with one more Poisson observation per season (after K seasons, mu_hat = K'/K with CI from chi-square). A media shock detected as a >3x weekly-volume deviation from the fitted mean path (exchange 8) triggers a volume-process update (add a new step indicator) but no change to the classification coefficients, since shocks inflate volume without inflating true positives. Parameter table (empirical inputs used by the update schedule): monthly_field_capacity = 40 investigations/month, interval [20, 60], up to ~100 in surge; source: expert exchange 3. response_freshness_window = act within 1-3 days, stale beyond ~1 week (7 days used); source: expert exchanges 5 and 10. update_cadence = daily re-scoring in active season (May-Oct), weekly in winter, re-estimate on >=3 new positives or >=100 new negatives or any new confirmed cluster; source: expert exchange 10. media_shock_trigger = weekly volume > 3x the fitted mean path adds a step indicator, classification coefficients unchanged; source: expert exchange 8. seasonal_carryover = carry coefficients across winter, re-center cluster set on prior season, no reset; source: expert exchange 9.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Update rules: (1) Daily (active season): s_i(t+1) = p_i(t) * (1 + 0.5*f_i(t+1)) * (1 + 0.5*n_i(t+1)); f_i uses the current date, so stale reports automatically sink; deploy top C. (2) On each new confirmation: add its location to the cluster set, recompute n_i for all open reports, re-rank immediately (exchange 10). (3) Refit threshold: |delta_verified| with >=3 new positives or >=100 new negatives; refit by L2-IRLS with CV over the expanded labeled set; accept the new coefficients only if 5-fold CV AUC does not drop by more than 0.02 (a guard against overfitting to a small new batch). (4) Per-season: mu update - after observing k' clusters in K seasons, mu_hat = k'/K, 95% CI [chi2(0.025, 2k')/2, chi2(0.975, 2k')/2]; after 2020 (k'=2, K=2): [0.24, 5.57]; after a zero-discovery 2021 season: k'=2, K=3 -> mu_hat = 0.67, CI [0.15, 3.41], which directly tightens the eradication evidence (subtask 5). (5) Shock detection: flag week t if y_t > 3 * mu_hat_t (the fitted mean path); then add I_t to the volume model and re-estimate the shock coefficient; classification coefficients unchanged. (6) Feature-drift monitor: track the base rate of 'has photo' among new reports; a sustained shift (e.g., a mobile app with camera capture raising it above ~20%) changes the label-selection mechanism and requires refitting with the new prevalence, since x_img's coefficient was estimated under the 98%-of-negatives-have-photo selection regime.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The cadence is deliberately asymmetric: the quantity that must track daily is the triage list (because opportunity decays in 1-7 days), while the statistical model is only re-estimated when the label set or the cluster set changes materially. This matches operational practice (exchange 10: daily triage and re-ranking, batched field deployment) and keeps the expensive step (refit + CV) to a few times per season. Quantitatively, a zero-discovery 2021 season would move the discovery-rate 95% CI from [0.24, 5.57] to [0.15, 3.41] and the next-season P(0 clusters) from 0.368 to 0.51, compounding the eradication evidence each season (subtask 5). Limitations: the >=3-positives refit rule is a heuristic - with n_pos=14 the model is not yet in a regime where incremental learning is safe, so early updates should be monitored via the CV-AUC guard; the 3x shock threshold is a conventional outlier rule, not an optimal detection rule; and the label-lag means a refit always slightly lags reality, which is why confirmation-triggered re-ranking (Tier 1) carries the time-critical part.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 5: State, using the model, what evidence would constitute eradication of Vespa mandarinia in Washington State.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) eradication means no surviving breeding population, and the operative stochastic quantity is the per-season number of discoverable colonies; (ii) evidence must be judged against maintained active surveillance, not passive absence of reports - if surveillance lapses, a zero-detection season does not count (expert exchange 6); (iii) the detection process has two channels: the passive channel measured by the data (public reports -> lab positives; the in-range passive positive rate is 9/152 = 0.059, Wilson 95% CI [0.0315, 0.1087]) and the active channel (trapping, sentinel hives, targeted searches; exchange 6) whose sensitivity is not in the dataset, so we bound the passive channel and state the active-channel requirement explicitly; (iv) the discovery process fitted in subtask 1, N_season ~ Poisson(mu) with mu_hat = 1.0 and 95% CI [0.24, 5.57], is the spread statistic against which zero-detection runs are evaluated; (v) the multi-year requirement is 2-3 seasons (exchange 6's typical 3, range 2-5), which we cross-check against the fitted Poisson rather than adopting by authority. Parameter table (empirical inputs): eradication_zero_seasons = 2 full active seasons of maintained surveillance (3 if reduced), policy range 2-5; source: expert exchange 6, cross-checked against the fitted Poisson below. inrange_passive_positive_rate = 9/152 = 0.059, Wilson 95% CI [0.0315, 0.1087]; source: task dataset (2020 labeled reports within 30 km of a confirmed cluster). cluster_discovery_rate mu = 1.0/season, 95% CI [0.24, 5.57]; source: task dataset. queen_founding_range = 30 km; source: problem statement. active_surveillance_requirement = trapping/sentinel hives maintained through the zero-run; a surveillance lapse voids the season; source: expert exchange 6.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Under N_season ~ Poisson(mu), K consecutive zero-discovery seasons give P(0 in K seasons | mu) = exp(-K*mu). Inverting P = 0.05: K=1 rules out mu >= 3.00; K=2 rules out mu >= 1.50; K=3 rules out mu >= 1.00 (the MLE). Since the current 95% CI upper end is 5.57, one maintained-surveillance zero season rules out mu > 3.0 (i.e., more than a third of the CI upper end), two zero seasons rule out mu > 1.5 (the geometric mean of the CI), and three zero seasons rule out mu > 1.0, the entire MLE - at which point the data are consistent only with a discovery rate at or below the MLE and the population is statistically implausible as an established breeding population. Equivalently, with the per-season detection model, two full active seasons (April-October) of maintained surveillance - active trapping plus the public-report channel running at or above its observed in-range sensitivity of 0.059 (CI [0.032, 0.109]) per in-range report, i.e. the passive channel alone would have caught a surviving in-range colony with probability 1-(1-0.059*n_reports)^season - with zero confirmed colonies constitute strong eradication evidence; three seasons if surveillance intensity is reduced (the exchange-6 typical value). Operational signature of 'not eradicated': any single confirmed positive after the run ends the zero-count (exchange 9: a spring re-detection is the same population continuing, so the clock does not merely pause - a confirmation restarts the active phase), or two or more corroborated in-range reports in a season without a confirmation (a warning state: escalate to active trapping before the zero-run is declared broken).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model-based eradication standard is: >= 2 consecutive full active seasons (3 if surveillance is reduced) of (a) maintained active surveillance at or above the sensitivity implied by the observed passive in-range capture rate (0.059 per in-range report, CI [0.032, 0.109]), (b) the public-report channel still receiving volume (a dead helpline is a surveillance lapse, not evidence), and (c) zero confirmed colonies, with the discovery-rate posterior updated each season (each zero season tightens the 95% CI: after one, [0.15, 3.41]). At the end of two such seasons, P(the true discovery rate exceeds 1.5/season) < 0.05, and at the end of three, P(it exceeds the observed MLE of 1.0/season) < 0.05 - that is the quantitative content of 'eradicated to 95% confidence' given the data's information content. Limitations: (i) with only two seasons of history, the Poisson CI is wide and the zero-run inversion is dominated by the CI upper end, so the standard is conservative by construction; (ii) the active-channel sensitivity is not in the dataset - if trapping plus sentinel hives detects surviving queens far better than the passive 0.059 in-range rate, the required zero-run shortens toward 2 seasons, and the standard should be re-estimated once a season of active-trap data exists; (iii) eradication here is Washington State only - a continuing population in adjacent BC (the 2019 Nanaimo colony) is a re-introduction risk that the zero-run does not control, so the standard should be applied jointly with the BC program; (iv) the standard says nothing about a far, single new incursion from outside the continent, which would be a new invasion, not a failure of eradication.
